11.1What is an Algorithm?

An algorithm is a step-by-step procedure for solving a class of problems — not just one specific case.

python
# This only solves ONE specific case: comparing exactly two numbers def find_larger_number(n1, n2): if n1 >= n2: return n1 else: return n2 # This only solves for exactly three numbers def find_largest_number_among_three(n1, n2, n3): if n1 >= n2 and n1 >= n3: return n1 elif n2 >= n1 and n2 >= n3: return n2 else: return n3

Neither function works for a list of any length. An algorithm for "find the largest number" needs to work no matter how many numbers are given.

11.2Comparing Two Algorithms for the Same Problem

Here are two different algorithms that both correctly find the largest number in a list:

python
# Algorithm 1: for every number, check whether it's >= every other number def find_largest_number_1(num_list): for num in num_list: if larger_than_or_equal_to_all(num, num_list): return num return None def larger_than_or_equal_to_all(n, n_list): for m in n_list: if m > n: return False return True # Algorithm 2: keep track of the largest number seen so far def find_largest_number_2(num_list): if num_list == []: return None largest = num_list[0] for num in num_list: if num > largest: largest = num return largest

Both give the correct answer — but find_largest_number_1 takes noticeably longer to run on a large list. This is what computational efficiency measures: not whether code works, but how well it scales as the input grows.

11.3Counting Basic Operations

To compare algorithms rigorously, we count the number of basic operations they perform, in terms of the input size (usually called n or l):

  • Variable assignment — assigning or updating a value
  • Arithmetic operations — e.g. addition, multiplication
  • Comparison — comparing two values
  • List or string indexing — accessing an element by its index

We usually count the worst case — the maximum number of operations the algorithm could need.

python
def find_largest_number_2(num_list): largest = num_list[0] # 1 assignment for num in num_list: # runs l times if num > largest: # l comparisons total largest = num # up to l-1 assignments return largest

For a list of length l, this performs about 2l operations — this is called a linear time algorithm, because the number of operations grows linearly (in direct proportion) with l.

Compare this with find_largest_number_1: for each of the l numbers, it calls larger_than_or_equal_to_all, which itself checks up to l numbers. In the worst case that's l * l, or l², operations — this is a quadratic time algorithm.

When l is small the difference barely matters, but when l is large (say, 20,000), l² becomes far bigger than 2l — which is why find_largest_number_1 is so much slower in practice.

11.4Asymptotic Behaviour & the Dominant Term

When comparing algorithms, we care about what happens as the input size grows very large (asymptotic behaviour). At that scale, constants and smaller terms stop mattering:

python
# 2n + 3 → as n grows, the "+3" becomes irrelevant → treat as O(n) # n² + n → the n² term grows much faster than n → treat as O(n²)

The fastest-growing term in the formula is called the dominant term, and it alone determines the algorithm's complexity.

11.5Big O Notation

Big O notation is used to describe an algorithm's worst-case complexity using its dominant term:

NameBig ORemarks
ConstantO(1)Not affected by input size n
LinearO(n)Running time is proportional to n; if n doubles, operations roughly double
PolynomialO(n^k)E.g. O(n²) — if n doubles, operations roughly quadruple
ExponentialO(k^n)E.g. O(2ⁿ) — if n increases by 1, operations roughly double
python
def get_first_element(lst): return lst[0] # O(1): always exactly one operation def linear_search(lst, target): for item in lst: # O(n): may need to check every item if item == target: return True return False
🧩 Pause & recall — What is the Big O of 3n² + 5n + 10?
Answer: O(n²). Drop constants and lower-order terms.
11.6Worked Example: Bubble Sort — O(n²)

Bubble Sort repeatedly steps through a list, swapping adjacent items that are in the wrong order, until the list is sorted:

python
def bubble_sort(lst): n = len(lst) for i in range(n): for j in range(0, n - i - 1): if lst[j] > lst[j + 1]: lst[j], lst[j + 1] = lst[j + 1], lst[j] return lst

The outer loop runs n times, and for each pass the inner loop runs roughly n times too — so in the worst case Bubble Sort performs about n * n = n² comparisons. That makes it an O(n²) algorithm, just like find_largest_number_1 above.

11.7Quick Rules of Thumb
  • 🔢 A single loop through the input → usually O(n)
  • 🔁 A loop inside a loop (both depending on n) → usually O(n²)
  • 🧹 Drop constants and lower-order terms: O(3n² + 5n + 10) → O(n²)
  • 🏆 When multiple terms are added together, only the dominant (fastest-growing) term matters: O(2ⁿ + n²) → O(2ⁿ)

(Note: exponential complexity is included above for completeness, but a full analysis of O(2ⁿ) cases is more advanced than this course covers.)

Part A. a/b - c/d = (a·d - b·c) / (b·d). The sign of the result is the sign of the numerator times the sign of the denominator, so we only need integers. Making both denominators positive first keeps the test simple.

python
def fraction_compare(fraction_1, fraction_2): a, b = fraction_1 c, d = fraction_2 if b < 0: a, b = -a, -b # move the sign to the numerator if d < 0: c, d = -c, -d diff = a * d - b * c # b and d are now positive if diff > 0: return 1 elif diff < 0: return -1 return 0

wr.q: Social people. meetups is a list of (person1, person2, date) where date is a negative integer (days ago). Write get_social_people(meetups, m, n) returning the people who met at least m different people in the past n days (dates -1, -2, ..., -n). The order of the two names in a tuple does not matter, and the same pair may appear many times.

Solution worked out for this guide (the paper has no answer key) and run against the examples in the question.

Build a dictionary from each person to the set of different people they met within the last n days. A set ignores repeats, so meeting the same friend twice counts once. Record the meeting for both people.

def get_social_people(meetups, m, n): friends = {} for p1, p2, day in meetups: if -n <= day <= -1: if p1 not in friends: friends[p1] = set() if p2 not in friends: friends[p2] = set() friends[p1].add(p2) friends[p2].add(p1) result = [] for person, met in friends.items(): if len(met) >= m: result.append(person) return result

Checks against the examples: (…, 2, 3) gives ['eric', 'jack']; (…, 3, 5) gives ['eric']; (…, 3, 1) gives [].

Marking points: date filter -n <= day <= -1; both directions recorded; duplicates ignored (set, or if x not in list); count of different friends compared with m; list of names returned.

Without sets, store a list per person and append only if the friend is not already in it.
